messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When the sheriff’s deputy, a young park ranger named Ethan, was pulled into a cramped interrogation room at the edge of a national forest, the air smelled of sweat and rust. They bound his arms to a wooden chair, cut a strip of leather across his chest, and began a series of electric shocks that rang in his ears like thunder. He could recall the instant the first jolt hit, the taste of metal on his tongue, the way his eyes were squeezed shut, but then a blankness swallowed the moments that followed. He was left with a jagged memory—some seconds crisp, others a void—and a conviction that his body had been permanently scarred by the violence. He could not rely on others; he feared that if he sought help, he would lose his mind. The night after the torture, Ethan spent hours rehearsing what he would say to anyone who might encounter him. He whispered phrases into the mirror, mentally repeating apologies and assurances. He had come to believe that his body was fragile and that his thoughts could not keep his past from catching up. The rehearsals gave him a fleeting sense of control, but they also hardened his belief that he could never trust anyone else. This conviction amplified the threat that lurked in every silence and every delayed response, and he began to check every lock on his car and his cabin, convinced that a new shock might be imminent. Each time he rehearsed, his mind forced the memory of the torture back into view, and the memory fed his sense of physical vulnerability, closing a loop that tightened with each passing day. Ethan’s work as a ranger placed him in a world of open roads and solitary trails. Driving through the park’s winding routes had become an avoidance that weighed on him heavily; he would turn off the highway and walk the rest of the distance, and if he had to drive, he would sit in the front seat and keep his back turned toward the road. The moment he was behind the wheel, a surge of panic would rise in his chest, as though a trigger had pulled a string of an old device. The delays that come with the unpredictable weather of the forest—such as a sudden storm that stalled his patrol—would provoke a flashback to the electric shock, and his body would react before he could think, a primal warning of impending danger. The memory would flare again, and the threat would swell, making him feel as if the past had become a living, breathing entity in the present. In the weeks that followed, the threat of an unexpected encounter made Ethan’s heart pound in his ears, and his body would tense as if ready for an unseen assailant. The memory of his torture would surface whenever a siren wailed in the distance or a wind gust sounded like the crack of a lever. Each trigger pulled him back into the scene of that night, reinforcing the belief that his body could never again be safe. He would sit at the ranger station, eyes darting, waiting for the doors to lock, while rehearsing the exact words he would say to his supervisor the next time he saw him. The rehearsals, in turn, forced his mind to replay the image of the leather strip and the jolt, further solidifying the memory and the threat it carried. Ethan felt his self‑esteem erode as he grew more dependent on the rehearsals, his ability to rely on others slipping away like fog. Now, after an incident in which a sudden, icy patch on the trail forced his car to skid and come to a halt in the middle of the forest, Ethan felt a wave of terror that was almost identical to the shock he had endured years ago. His heart pounded, he saw flashes of that night, and his mind was flooded with the realization that his avoidance of driving was robbing him of his job, his purpose. He had reached a tipping point; the avoidance was no longer a defense but a cage. With trembling hands, he called a therapist, hoping to untangle the web of rehearsals, threat monitoring, and memory that had bound his life. He fears that if he does not break this cycle, he will be trapped forever in a state of hypervigilance, unable to trust others or even himself, but he also holds a fragile hope that through treatment he can reclaim a life where the past no longer dictates the future.
